newsitem.title: CHINA: Jardine executives fete HK handover in style.
newsitem.headline: Jardine executives fete HK handover in style.

text.p: Champagne flowed and a disco throbbed "Mission Impossible" as captains of Hong Kong industry made their leap from buccaneer capitalism to an uncertain future under Chinese communism.
For Jardine Matheson, the noble house famed for its taipans who run the conglomerate known as the "Princely Hong", it truly was a historic moment.

In the 48th floor penthouse of Jardine Matheson, whose buccaneer founders have been inextricably linked with Hong Kong since 1841, the music was turned off and a giant television screen on at midnight when British rule ended.
As sober-suited executives contemplated their future under China, Anthony Nightingale, a Jardine Matheson director, offered a toast to the new Special Administrative Region.
Within minutes, the throbbing disco had started up again and young executives were back on the floor with white-gloved waiters dancing attendance with the champagne.
Jardine and Matheson are names synonymous with the opium trade which led to war between Britain and China and resulted in the British seizing Hong Kong at gunpoint in 1841.
Beijing once condemned Jardine as "the black sheep of business".

Jardine, Hong Kong's largest private-sector employer, angered Beijing when it shifted its domicile from Hong Kong to Bermuda in 1984 when the ink was barely dry on the Sino-British declaration that spelled an end to London's rule of Hong Kong.
But in May, Jardine chairman Henry Keswick shook the hand of China's economic czar, vice-premier Zhu Rongji.
The "Princely Hong" had come in from the cold.

Out on the windswept terrace of the penthouse, Jardine executives contemplated the future against a magnificent backdrop -- the Peak shrouded in mist, the harbour encircled by a necklace of glittering skyscrapers and the Royal Yacht Britannia about to sail into history.
Jardine's finance director, Norman Lyle, was in a reflective but confident mood as he gazed at the stunning scene.
"The future is here. We have been here for 165 years," he said as the curtain went down on Britain's empire east of Suez.
"Just look at this marvellous scene -- lights, buildings and all this prosperity."
